idiom_name: tarn.js Pool<T> (or generic-pool with its typings)
implementation_notes: TypeScript's answer to the same need is a typed pool library: tarn.js - written in TypeScript and used by Knex - takes create/destroy/validate callbacks and puts a timeout on every operation that can fail (acquireTimeoutMillis, createTimeoutMillis, destroyTimeoutMillis) so a hanging factory cannot fill the pool with dead entries; acquire() returns an object with a promise and an abort() method, release() returns the resource, and numUsed/numFree/numPendingAcquires expose saturation. Because the library ships its own typings, the resource type flows through the pool and the factory callbacks are checked at compile time, so the structural part of the pattern (free list, wait queue, eviction, timeouts) is entirely library-owned; hand-roll only for semantics the library does not model, such as per-tenant sub-pools.
pitfalls: Types do not enforce the lease: TypeScript cannot make release() mandatory, so wrap acquire in a helper returning [resource, release] or a template that always releases in a finally.
`strict` and readonly do not create linearity - a resource can still be used after release, and the compiler will not object; the discipline is architectural, not type-level.
The runtime is still Node: evictor timers, open handles and the need to drain/de-register shutdown hooks are identical to the JavaScript case.
